title: Declining anthropogenic aerosols amplify Northern Hemisphere Hadley circulation weakening in the 21st century

paper_content.abstract:
The Hadley circulation plays a key role in transporting atmospheric heat from the tropics to the
subtropics, shaping the climate in low latitudes. While its projected weakening has been largely
attributed to rising greenhouse gas concentrations, the long-term impact of future anthropogenic
aerosol concentrations remains underexplored. Here, we show that the projected changes in
anthropogenic aerosol concentrations can account for about one-third of the Northern Hemisphere
Hadley circulation weakening between 1980 and 2080, emerging as a major driver of tropical
circulation change throughout the 21st century. This impact is linked to altered diabatic heating
patterns in the northern tropics, driven by precipitation changes under reduced aerosol forcing.
These results highlight a critical trade-off of aerosol mitigation: while improving air quality, it may
amplify tropical atmospheric circulation changes driven by greenhouse gases.
paper_content.introduction:
The Hadley Circulation (HC) consists of ascending motion in the deep tropics, poleward flow in
the upper troposphere, descending motion in the subtropics, and equatorward return flow near the
surface. This thermally direct overturning circulation strongly influences tropical hydroclimate
and maintains subtropical dry zones1–4. As global warming accelerates, climate model simulations
consistently project a weakening of the Northern Hemisphere (NH) HC from the past to the future
climate5–9. This weakening has primarily been attributed to changes in anthropogenic greenhouse
gases and aerosols6,10–17.

While the weakening of the HC by increasing greenhouse gases is well documented, the response
of the HC to changing aerosols is not well understood as it is sensitive to the analysis period and
models due to the complex spatiotemporal evolution of aerosol forcing10,15,18. Anthropogenic
aerosols increased globally until the 1980s, particularly after the end of World War II, but have
since followed divergent regional trajectories: declining in Europe and North America due to
effective mitigation efforts but continuing to increase in East and South Asia19–24 (Supplementary
Fig. 1). Past studies utilizing climate model simulations in different configurations have shown
that the overall cooling effect of increasing anthropogenic aerosols has likely strengthened the HC
in the NH, counteracting the weakening induced by greenhouse warming10,17,25. However, the
impacts of anthropogenic aerosols over the past few decades are uncertain, as aerosol
concentrations have declined in the Western Hemisphere but increased in the Eastern Hemisphere.
While these zonally asymmetric aerosol forcings may have competed with each other, recent
studies have suggested that changes in HC intensity are more sensitive to aerosol changes in the
Western Hemisphere, thereby driving a likely weakening of the HC since the 1980s16,21,23. Despite
these findings, the impact of time-varying aerosol forcings (Supplementary Fig. 1) on HC intensity
change is not well quantified. The relative importance of anthropogenic aerosols compared to
greenhouse gases and their underlying mechanism(s) also remains poorly understood.

In this work, we show the pivotal role of anthropogenic aerosol forcing in driving intensity changes
of the NH HC. By examining large ensembles of single-forcing climate model simulations, we
identify the mechanisms underlying aerosol-induced HC intensity changes and compare them with
those driven by greenhouse gases. As the impacts of aerosols on atmospheric circulation changes
are often obscure and model-dependent26–28, the robustness of the results is also tested by
employing a multi-model framework and an additional suite of the latest large-ensemble
simulations.

differences in aerosol distributions and stratospheric ozone27,32.

The intensity of the NH HC (hereafter referred to as HC unless otherwise specified) exhibits a
distinct decadal variation (Fig. 1a). Specifically, the trend switches sign around 1980, transitioning
from a strengthening phase prior to the 1970s to a weakening phase thereafter (Table 1). The recent
weakening is consistent with observations5, although it is less clear in reanalyses33,34. As shown
below, this transition is likely associated with changes in aerosol emissions in the NH
(Supplementary Fig. 1; See also refs.16,23,35,36).

The contribution of increasing greenhouse gas concentrations to the HC intensity change is
quantified by taking a difference between ALL and fixed greenhouse gas concentrations (XGHG)
experiments, denoted as GHG experiment (red in Fig. 1c; See Methods). The HC intensity trend
in GHG experiment is statistically significant over the analysis period (1920–2080) but is smaller
than the trend in ALL experiment. Even during the period of 1980–2080 when greenhouse-gas-
induced HC weakening accelerates, the trend is only ~60% of that in ALL experiment (Table 1).
The time of emergence in GHG experiment is also delayed by about 20 years compared to that in
ALL experiment (compare crossing of green lines in Fig. 1c with Fig. 1a). This suggests that
increasing greenhouse gases do not fully explain the HC weakening in ALL experiment, indicating
a substantial influence of anthropogenic aerosols.

The contribution of anthropogenic aerosols is quantified by differencing ALL from fixed
anthropogenic aerosols (XAER) experiments, denoted as AER (blue in Fig. 1c; See Methods).
While the aerosol-induced HC intensity change lies within the natural variability for the entire
period (1920–2080), statistically significant trends are observed in two distinct sub-periods (Table
1): the earlier period (1920–1980) when anthropogenic aerosols increased globally
(Supplementary Fig. 1), and the subsequent period (1981–2080) of anthropogenic aerosols decline,
especially in the Western Hemisphere36. During 1920–1980, increasing aerosol concentrations
strengthened the HC intensity by 0.47×109 kg s-1decade-1, which exceeds the trend in the ALL
experiment. After 1980, declining aerosol concentrations weaken the HC by -0.35×109 kg s-1
decade-1, accounting for approximately 34% of the total HC weakening in the ALL experiment
over 1980–2080 (Table 1). Since the latter weakening effect after 1980 outweighs the former
strengthening effect before 1980, the net impact of anthropogenic aerosol forcing on HC intensity
over the entire analysis period is an overall weakening (Table 1). The results are robust to the
specific choice of transition year within the 1970–1980 period, as NH aerosol emissions were in a
transition phase during this decade (Supplementary Fig. 1).

It is important to note that aerosol effect is not always secondary. In certain periods, it acts as the
dominant driver of HC intensity changes. For instance, during the earlier phase of aerosol decline
(1980–2040), the aerosol-induced HC weakening (-0.56109 kg s-1 decade-1) is more pronounced
than the greenhouse-gas-induced weakening (-0.34109 kg s-1 decade-1). This underscores the
time-dependent nature of aerosol forcing and its critical role in shaping near-term tropical
circulation changes.

The combined effects of greenhouse gases and aerosols are further evaluated by comparing the
trend derived from the linear sum of the GHG and AER experiments (GHG + AER; purple in Fig.
1c) with that from the ALL experiment (black in Fig. 1a). The two time series are quantitatively
similar, showing close agreement across the three investigated periods (Table 1). This result
indicates that anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols are the two primary factors governing
the HC intensity changes from 1920 to 2080, consistent with ref.36.

The above results, derived from a single model, are supported by multi-model analyses. The multi-
model mean from the models participating in the CMIP6 Detection and Attribution Model
Intercomparison Project (DAMIP; See Methods)37 shows qualitatively similar results, despite
different experiment design and aerosol forcing (Table 1; See also Supplementary Fig. 3). In all-
forcing experiments, HC intensity exhibits a slight strengthening during 1920–1980, followed by
a weakening during 1980–2080. Approximately 26% of HC weakening is attributed to aerosol
reductions: -1.13×109 kg s-1 decade-1 in all forcing experiments versus -0.29×109 kg s-1 decade-1
in aerosol-only experiments over 1980–2080.

The robustness of HC intensity changes is also tested by examining the latest CESM2 large
ensemble single-forcing experiment (CESM2 LENS; See Methods). This experiment differs from
CESM1 LENS in that greenhouse gas or aerosol forcings are prescribed with all other forcings
held fixed at the 1850’s levels. Despite this difference, as well as differences in aerosol emission
scenarios, ensemble size, and integration length, qualitatively similar results are obtained
(Supplementary Fig. 4). The anthropogenic aerosol-only experiment in CESM2 LENS shows a
statistically significant HC strengthening of 0.43109 kg s-1 decade-1 for 1920–1980, and a
subsequent weakening of -0.48109 kg s-1 decade-1 for 1980–2050. This result is consistent with
the findings from both CESM1 LENS and CMIP6 DAMIP results (Table 1).

CESM1 LENS

A set of CESM1 55 large ensemble (LENS) simulations with a 1° spatial resolution 36 is analyzed
in this study. These simulations consist of 1) a 40-member ensemble simulation with all forcings
(ALL), 2) a 20-member ensemble simulation with time-fixed aerosol concentrations (XAER), and
3) a 20-member ensemble simulation with time-fixed greenhouse gas concentrations (XGHG).
Each ensemble member in XGHG and XAER experiments is initialized in the same manner in
ALL experiment. ALL experiment is forced by historical forcings for the period 1920–2005 and
by the CMIP5 RCP8.5 scenario for the period 2006–210053. Both XGHG and XAER experiments
use the same forcing protocol, except that either greenhouse gas or aerosol concentrations are held
fixed at the 1920’s condition. The temporal evolution of global-mean surface air temperature from
1920 to 2080 is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 8. ALL experiment shows a steady warming
trend from the past to the future, being the warming intensity sensitive to the period. The warming
before the year 1980 is much weaker than the one afterward, with a large variability. The warming
trend in ALL experiment (-0.62 K decade-1) is well captured by the linear sum of the GHG and
AER experiments (GHG+AER; -0.62 K decade-1), supporting the use of these experiments to
attribute forced responses. They are compared to an 1800-year pre-industrial control simulation
(piControl), which is used to estimate the internal climate variability.

The impacts of greenhouse gases and aerosols forcings on the past and future changes in the HC
intensity are quantified by computing the ensemble-mean differences between the two experiments,
i.e., ALL-XAER (referred to as AER experiment) and ALL-XGHG (referred to as GHG
experiment). AER experiment isolates the effect of aerosol forcing, while the GHG experiment
isolates that of greenhouse gas forcing. Although 40 members are available for ALL experiment,
only the first 20 members are analyzed to make a fair comparison to XGHG and XAER experiment.
The results from all 40 ensemble members in ALL experiment are quantitatively the same as those
from the first 20 members (Compare Fig. 1a to Supplementary Fig. 9)

CESM2 LENS

A set of CESM2 LENS simulations56 is also examined. They differ from CESM1 LENS
simulations not only in model but also in experiment design. While CESM1 LENS uses an all-
but-one framework (i.e., XGHG and XAER), CESM2 LENS uses a forcing-only framework.
CESM2 single-forcing LENS simulations consist of 20 ensemble members of anthropogenic
aerosol-only (AAER) experiments, and 15 ensemble members of greenhouse gas-only (GHG)
experiments. To maintain consistency, the first 15 ensembles from both experiments are analyzed.
Each experiment spans from 1920 to 2050, which is shorter than the period covered by CESM1
LENS, based on historical (1920–2014) and SSP3-7.0 (2015–2050) scenarios.

Although CESM2 LENS is the latest single-forcing large ensemble experiments, this study
primarily analyses CESM1-LENS. This is because it has a longer temporal coverage (extending
to 2080) and larger ensemble size (20 members), both of which are essential for robustly detecting
long-term forced responses and identifying the underlying physical mechanisms.

CMIP6 DAMIP

In addition to CESM1 LENS, we use model output from the Detection and Attribution Model
Intercomparison Project (DAMIP)37 of CMIP657. DAMIP provides single-forcing simulations that
isolate the effects of individual forcing agents, including anthropogenic aerosols and greenhouse
gases, in both historical and future climates. This dataset allows us to assess whether the HC
response to aerosol forcings is consistent across a broader set of models. Specifically, four models
which provide both the historical aerosol-only (hist-aer) and GHG-only (hist-GHG) simulations
for 1850–2020, as well as their respective future scenarios (ssp245-aer and ssp245-GHG) for
2021–2100, are used. They are CanESM5, GISS-E2-1-G, MIROC6, and NorESM2-LM. Historical
simulation for 1850–2014 and SSP2-4.5 scenario simulation for 2015–2100 are also examined to
provide a more comprehensive comparison with CESM1 LENS. For consistency, only the first
ensemble member from each model (r1i1p1f2 for GISS-E2-1-G and r1i1p1f1 for the others) is
used for the common period 1920–2080 for a direct comparison among the simulations. Although
one ensemble member from each model is utilized to avoid overpresentation of models with larger
ensembles, the results do not change significantly when all available ensemble members are used.

It is important to note that the aerosol scenarios differ between the model experiments. DAMIP
follows the SSP2-4.5 aerosol pathway, while XAER experiment in CESM1 LENS and aerosol-
only experiment in CESM2 LENS are based on the RCP8.5 and SSP3-7.0 aerosol scenarios,
respectively. As such, comparisons between CESM1 LENS, CESM2 LENS, and DAMIP should
be interpreted qualitatively.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I have completed my review of “Anthropogenic Aerosol Decline Substantially Amplifies Northern Hadley Circulation Weakening in the 21st century” by S.-Y. Kim et. al., submitted 2025 to Nature Communications.
In the study, the authors first quantify the change in the strength of the northern- and southern-hemisphere Hadley Circulation (HC) under historic and projected aerosol, greenhouse gas, and all-forcing scenarios in the CESM1 large ensemble. The authors find that the northern HC weakens under the all-forcing scenario from 1920-2080, while the change in the southern HC is indistinguishable from natural variability. They attribute this decline in the northern hemisphere HC to a combination of GHG and anthropogenic forcings through use of the CESM1 single-forcing large ensemble simulations. Further analysis of the CMIP6 Detection and Attribution Model Intercomparison Project (DAMIP) shows qualitatively similar results, but of a smaller magnitude.
The authors then utilize a Kuo-Eliassen decomposition to separate changes in the overturning streamfunction into contributions from diabatic heating, eddy heat flux, eddy momentum flux, zonal friction terms, and changes in static stability. This decomposition method was then applied to the various CESM1 Large Ensemble simulations. Differences in the components between the ALL, GHG, and AER configurations were then compared.
I found the analysis contained within the study to be sound and that the topic potentially falls within the scope of Nature Communications. However this manuscript does not clearly articulate the key result(s) of the study, and how they are significant to the field. Therefore I recommend a major revision before this manuscript is accepted for publication. I have included additional comments below that I hope the authors will use to strengthen the manuscript.
----------------
General Comments
----------------
As written, the primary conclusion seems to be that past and future changes in aerosol forcing lead to a change in the strength of the northern hemisphere Hadley circulation. This is not a particularly novel result, and has been explicitly discussed (or implied, through discussion of e.g., atmospheric heat transport or ITCZ shifts) in various studies including:
* Ming, Y., and V. Ramaswamy, 2011: A model investigation of aerosol-induced changes in tropical circulation. J. Climate, 24, 5125–5133, https://doi.org/10.1175/2011JCLI4108.1.
* Hwang, Y.-T., D. M. W. Frierson, and S. M. Kang, 2013: Anthropogenic sulfate aerosol and the southward shift of tropical precipitation in the late 20th century. Geophys. Res. Lett., 40, 2845–2850, https://doi.org/10.1002/grl.50502.
* Kang, S. M., 2020: Extratropical influence on the tropical rainfall distribution. Curr. Climate Change Rep., 6, 24–36, https://doi.org/10.1007/s40641-020-00154-y.
* Needham et. al., 2024: Aerosol-Induced Changes in Atmospheric and Oceanic Heat Transports in the CESM2 Large Ensemble. J. Climate, 37, 6395-6412, https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-23-0455.1
In other words, I am not surprised to see a significant trend in the NH HC under the ALL-xAER scenario. Instead, I am much more interested in why this would be the case.
I believe that the authors’ use of the Kuo-Eliassen equation is useful perspective from which to address this question. I would encourage the authors to consider how they could rework their discussion (i.e., of Fig. 2) to relate changes in these KE terms to real, physical phenomena in the atmosphere and oceans. Some of this has already been included (e.g., the diabatic heating term and precipitation). However, as I read the manuscript (particularly lines 118 – 173) I found myself constantly stopping and trying to reason through why a change in aerosol forcing would lead to a particular response to one of the KE terms.
-----------------
Specific Comments
-----------------
Line 39 “rose steadily”: may want to specify the initial time bounds. For example, “rose rapidly from the end of WWII until the 1970s”
Line 42: I found “unmask” to be a strange word choice. May be better served to rewrite this sentence to clarify that aerosol radiative forcing previously opposed/balanced GHG radiative forcing, but now aerosol forcing has diminished.
Lines 44-47: Should probably bring in some of the observational evidence of the tropical precipitation shift. For example, Hwang et al., 2013 "Anthropogenic sulfate aerosol and the southward shift of tropical precipitation in the late 20th century" and subsequent literature
Line 57-58: Any particular reason for the choice of the CESM1-LENS simulations when the CESM2-LENS simulations are available? For example, a preference for the all-but-one over the only-one experimental setup? Should probably at least comment on why you are using the older simulations.
Line 64: “ALL” has not been defined at this point in the text. Reference the methods?
Lines 67-68: Specifically on the “reversing an earlier strengthening” comment. This relates my general comment on how previous work has linked aerosol forcing to the 1970s era peak. The Needham et al. (2024) study referenced above explicitly discussed this in the context of a change in the streamfunction for CESM2-LENS simulations.
Line 74: Should briefly note the sign change as the reason to use PSImin vs PSImax in the SH
Line 109: “models show qualitatively similar results” is models the right word here, or should it instead be something like (e.g.,) “multi-model mean from multiple models under the same forcing scenario.”
Line 125: First instance of “KE,” should use the full name and maybe reference the methods section.
Lines 127-128: This is an opportunity to expand a bit on my general comment above. I would suggest briefly linking the diabatic heating term to precipitation which is discussed a bit later in the manuscript. This allows the reader to understand the physical interpretation of the mathematical quantity called “diabatic heating.” Many readers will be able to make the connection themselves. But explicilty linking the physical to the mathematical within the text helps guide the reader to consider the relationship between the hadley circulation and (in this case) precipitation. Similar comments could be made for the other terms. This then helps the reader interpret Fig 2 as physical quantities instead of simply as bars on a plot.
Lines 147-148: Similarly, a brief note about the relationship between S^2 and -dT/dp as seen in the methods section makes it clear to the reader why you are referencing Fig S4e.
Lines 157-159: The comment about the Northern Pacific may be unclear to some readers so consider supporting this statement with a citation
Line 169: Maybe clarify that “reduced Q” is relative to the All / GHG simulations
Lines 169-171: In Fig. S5 the “peak" in precipitation ~10N is pretty weak for the DAMIP simulations. But I see that the STD range narrows. Consider reevaluating this claim that the patterns are consistent to more precisely align with Fig S5.
Lines 177-178: This again relates to my general comment above. The NHC weakening has also been explained in the context of changes in anthropogenic aerosols in those previous studies I mentioned, and references therein.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors explore the potential influence of anthropogenic aerosol (AA) forcing on the Northern Hemisphere (NH) hadley cell weakening from 1970 to 2080 based on single forcing simulations from various climate models. Their analyses reveal that about 40% of the NH Hadley cell weakening is attributed to the decline in AA. Based on the KE equation decomposition, they further demonstrate that the weakening is linked to diabatic heating patterns asymmetrically placed in the two hemispheres.
The analyses based on KE equation is interesting, but I have a fundamental concern about this manuscript, where the authors seem to oversimplify the aerosol emission to be simply “decline” since 1970, which is a bit outdated compared to relevant studies published in recent years. It is true that the global-mean aerosol concentration has been continuously decreasing since the 1970s. However, the declines only occur in Europe and North America, while emissions in other regions, especially East and South Asia, kept increasing, which seems to be less discussed in the introduction. Actually, many of the cited studies discussing global-mean aerosol forcings were published about ten years ago, so some of the discussions on hemispheric aerosol imbalance seem to be outdated.
Many studies have emphasized the complex co-impacts of regional aerosol forcings due to the strong spatial heterogeneity (e.g., [1-8]), in that different regional aerosol forcings could have distinct teleconnections to the large-scale circulations. For example, the Hadley cell discussed in this manuscript is sensitive to the latitudinal locations of forcings, and the aerosol forcings in Asia and Europe since the 1970s are located at distinct zonal and meridional locations, which should have very different dynamical impacts on the Northern Hemisphere Hadley cell ([3]).
Moreover, since the authors also include the future projections up to 2080, it is worth noting that the emissions between East Asia and South Asia started to show different trends since the recent decade as well, which further increases the complexity (e.g., Ref.[9-11]). So recently many efforts have been made to diagnose the impacts of more aerosol forcings (e.g., RAMIP; [8-9]), and the RCP emission scenario seems to be outdated to diagnose the future impacts of aerosols.
Therefore, I am concerned that the authors’ attribution to “decline of aerosol forcing” oversimplified the dynamical mechanisms behind the large-scale circulation responses. Although the energy analyses are interesting, I am concerned this study might not be novel and robust enough to extend the current understanding of anthropogenic aerosols, to be honest….
Minor comments:
Line 37: The impact of aerosol on the Northern hemisphere HC was discussed in some studies (e.g., Ref[3, 5]).
Line 39 and many other places: The statement is misleading. “declined due to growing aerosol mitigation efforts” only occurred in North America and Europe as mentioned above. This should be clarified and emphasized here and there.
Line 106: Some recent studies have conducted inter-model comparisons of aerosol forcings (e.g., [10]), which are worth referring to.
Line 283: I think that CESM2 single forcing is still worth diagnosing in the authors’ setup. The aerosol emissions beyond 2050 are fairly small, so it does not matter that much if we stop at 2050. Also, CESM2 is more sensitive to aerosol forcings, which is debated to be unrealistic in some studies though. The differences between CESM1 and CESM as well as the caveat of CESM2 aerosol modules are worth discussing.
Line 291: I am not quite sure if I understand the authors’ argument correctly, but the claim of “one-to-one comparison between the experiments” are incorrect for me. Although the single forcing simulations are branched from the ALL experiment, they are different “worlds” when forcings are changed since the internal variability changes after the first few decades. So it is impossible to do a “one-to-one” comparison between ensemble members.
Line 292: Intuitively, all ensemble members are used when calculating forced responses to smooth out the impacts of internal variability as much as possible. It could be better if the authors could compare the results of ALL between using all members and using the first 20 members.
Line 317: Same as the previous comment. Intuitively, all ensemble members should be used to calculate the ensemble mean, in my opinion.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The Hadley circulation plays a key role in transporting atmospheric heat from the tropics to the
subtropics, shaping the climate in low latitudes. While its projected weakening has been largely
attributed to rising greenhouse gas concentrations, the long-term impact of future anthropogenic
aerosol concentrations remains underexplored. Here, we show that the projected changes in
anthropogenic aerosol concentrations can account for about one-third of the Northern Hemisphere
Hadley circulation weakening between 1980 and 2080, emerging as a major driver of tropical
circulation change throughout the 21st century. This impact is linked to altered diabatic heating
patterns in the northern tropics, driven by precipitation changes under reduced aerosol forcing.
These results highlight a critical trade-off of aerosol mitigation: while improving air quality, it may
amplify tropical atmospheric circulation changes driven by greenhouse gases.

---

## Introduction

The Hadley Circulation (HC) consists of ascending motion in the deep tropics, poleward flow in
the upper troposphere, descending motion in the subtropics, and equatorward return flow near the
surface. This thermally direct overturning circulation strongly influences tropical hydroclimate
and maintains subtropical dry zones1–4. As global warming accelerates, climate model simulations
consistently project a weakening of the Northern Hemisphere (NH) HC from the past to the future
climate5–9. This weakening has primarily been attributed to changes in anthropogenic greenhouse
gases and aerosols6,10–17.

While the weakening of the HC by increasing greenhouse gases is well documented, the response
of the HC to changing aerosols is not well understood as it is sensitive to the analysis period and
models due to the complex spatiotemporal evolution of aerosol forcing10,15,18. Anthropogenic
aerosols increased globally until the 1980s, particularly after the end of World War II, but have
since followed divergent regional trajectories: declining in Europe and North America due to
effective mitigation efforts but continuing to increase in East and South Asia19–24 (Supplementary
Fig. 1). Past studies utilizing climate model simulations in different configurations have shown
that the overall cooling effect of increasing anthropogenic aerosols has likely strengthened the HC
in the NH, counteracting the weakening induced by greenhouse warming10,17,25. However, the
impacts of anthropogenic aerosols over the past few decades are uncertain, as aerosol
concentrations have declined in the Western Hemisphere but increased in the Eastern Hemisphere.
While these zonally asymmetric aerosol forcings may have competed with each other, recent
studies have suggested that changes in HC intensity are more sensitive to aerosol changes in the
Western Hemisphere, thereby driving a likely weakening of the HC since the 1980s16,21,23. Despite
these findings, the impact of time-varying aerosol forcings (Supplementary Fig. 1) on HC intensity
change is not well quantified. The relative importance of anthropogenic aerosols compared to
greenhouse gases and their underlying mechanism(s) also remains poorly understood.

In this work, we show the pivotal role of anthropogenic aerosol forcing in driving intensity changes
of the NH HC. By examining large ensembles of single-forcing climate model simulations, we
identify the mechanisms underlying aerosol-induced HC intensity changes and compare them with
those driven by greenhouse gases. As the impacts of aerosols on atmospheric circulation changes
are often obscure and model-dependent26–28, the robustness of the results is also tested by
employing a multi-model framework and an additional suite of the latest large-ensemble
simulations.

---

## Results

Hadley circulation weakening due to anthropogenic forcings

The HC intensity changes, derived from the CESM1 large ensemble single-forcing experiment
(CESM1 LENS), are presented in Fig. 1. Under all-forcing scenario (ALL experiment; See
Methods), the NH HC intensity (Ψ ) shows robust weakening from 1920 to 2080 at a rate of -
max
0.62×109 kg s-1decade-1 (Table 1). This is consistent with a previous study6. The time of emergence
of NH HC intensity change, determined by the year when the forced response exceeds the range
of natural variability29–31, is estimated to be around 2020. The natural variability is defined as the
one-standard-deviation range of Ψ in the pre-industrial simulation (green lines in Fig. 1a).
max
The long-term change is less pronounced in the Southern Hemisphere (SH) HC intensity (Ψ ).
min
From 1920 through 2080, Ψ remains within the bounds of the internal variability (Fig. 1b). This
min
result reinforces the finding that the HC weakening is more pronounced in the NH than in the
SH6,12. This hemispheric asymmetry is consistent with prior studies and may be related to
differences in aerosol distributions and stratospheric ozone27,32.

The intensity of the NH HC (hereafter referred to as HC unless otherwise specified) exhibits a
distinct decadal variation (Fig. 1a). Specifically, the trend switches sign around 1980, transitioning
from a strengthening phase prior to the 1970s to a weakening phase thereafter (Table 1). The recent
weakening is consistent with observations5, although it is less clear in reanalyses33,34. As shown
below, this transition is likely associated with changes in aerosol emissions in the NH
(Supplementary Fig. 1; See also refs.16,23,35,36).

The contribution of increasing greenhouse gas concentrations to the HC intensity change is
quantified by taking a difference between ALL and fixed greenhouse gas concentrations (XGHG)
experiments, denoted as GHG experiment (red in Fig. 1c; See Methods). The HC intensity trend
in GHG experiment is statistically significant over the analysis period (1920–2080) but is smaller
than the trend in ALL experiment. Even during the period of 1980–2080 when greenhouse-gas-
induced HC weakening accelerates, the trend is only ~60% of that in ALL experiment (Table 1).
The time of emergence in GHG experiment is also delayed by about 20 years compared to that in
ALL experiment (compare crossing of green lines in Fig. 1c with Fig. 1a). This suggests that
increasing greenhouse gases do not fully explain the HC weakening in ALL experiment, indicating
a substantial influence of anthropogenic aerosols.

The contribution of anthropogenic aerosols is quantified by differencing ALL from fixed
anthropogenic aerosols (XAER) experiments, denoted as AER (blue in Fig. 1c; See Methods).
While the aerosol-induced HC intensity change lies within the natural variability for the entire
period (1920–2080), statistically significant trends are observed in two distinct sub-periods (Table
1): the earlier period (1920–1980) when anthropogenic aerosols increased globally
(Supplementary Fig. 1), and the subsequent period (1981–2080) of anthropogenic aerosols decline,
especially in the Western Hemisphere36. During 1920–1980, increasing aerosol concentrations
strengthened the HC intensity by 0.47×109 kg s-1decade-1, which exceeds the trend in the ALL
experiment. After 1980, declining aerosol concentrations weaken the HC by -0.35×109 kg s-1
decade-1, accounting for approximately 34% of the total HC weakening in the ALL experiment
over 1980–2080 (Table 1). Since the latter weakening effect after 1980 outweighs the former
strengthening effect before 1980, the net impact of anthropogenic aerosol forcing on HC intensity
over the entire analysis period is an overall weakening (Table 1). The results are robust to the
specific choice of transition year within the 1970–1980 period, as NH aerosol emissions were in a
transition phase during this decade (Supplementary Fig. 1).

It is important to note that aerosol effect is not always secondary. In certain periods, it acts as the
dominant driver of HC intensity changes. For instance, during the earlier phase of aerosol decline
(1980–2040), the aerosol-induced HC weakening (-0.56109 kg s-1 decade-1) is more pronounced
than the greenhouse-gas-induced weakening (-0.34109 kg s-1 decade-1). This underscores the
time-dependent nature of aerosol forcing and its critical role in shaping near-term tropical
circulation changes.

The combined effects of greenhouse gases and aerosols are further evaluated by comparing the
trend derived from the linear sum of the GHG and AER experiments (GHG + AER; purple in Fig.
1c) with that from the ALL experiment (black in Fig. 1a). The two time series are quantitatively
similar, showing close agreement across the three investigated periods (Table 1). This result
indicates that anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols are the two primary factors governing
the HC intensity changes from 1920 to 2080, consistent with ref.36.

The above results, derived from a single model, are supported by multi-model analyses. The multi-
model mean from the models participating in the CMIP6 Detection and Attribution Model
Intercomparison Project (DAMIP; See Methods)37 shows qualitatively similar results, despite
different experiment design and aerosol forcing (Table 1; See also Supplementary Fig. 3). In all-
forcing experiments, HC intensity exhibits a slight strengthening during 1920–1980, followed by
a weakening during 1980–2080. Approximately 26% of HC weakening is attributed to aerosol
reductions: -1.13×109 kg s-1 decade-1 in all forcing experiments versus -0.29×109 kg s-1 decade-1
in aerosol-only experiments over 1980–2080.

The robustness of HC intensity changes is also tested by examining the latest CESM2 large
ensemble single-forcing experiment (CESM2 LENS; See Methods). This experiment differs from
CESM1 LENS in that greenhouse gas or aerosol forcings are prescribed with all other forcings
held fixed at the 1850’s levels. Despite this difference, as well as differences in aerosol emission
scenarios, ensemble size, and integration length, qualitatively similar results are obtained
(Supplementary Fig. 4). The anthropogenic aerosol-only experiment in CESM2 LENS shows a
statistically significant HC strengthening of 0.43109 kg s-1 decade-1 for 1920–1980, and a
subsequent weakening of -0.48109 kg s-1 decade-1 for 1980–2050. This result is consistent with
the findings from both CESM1 LENS and CMIP6 DAMIP results (Table 1).

Physical processes of Hadley circulation weakening

While both increasing greenhouse gas concentrations and decreasing aerosol concentrations
contribute to the HC weakening during 1980–2080, their underlying mechanisms may differ. The
latitudinal-pressure structure of mass streamfunction (Ψ) indeed shows distinctively different
responses of the HC to the two forcings (Supplementary Fig. 2). Greenhouse gas forcing leads to

forcing causes weakening primarily in the deep tropics within ~15° N (Supplementary Fig. 2f).

A set of CESM1 55 large ensemble (LENS) simulations with a 1° spatial resolution 36 is analyzed
in this study. These simulations consist of 1) a 40-member ensemble simulation with all forcings

3) a 20-member ensemble simulation with time-fixed greenhouse gas concentrations (XGHG).
Each ensemble member in XGHG and XAER experiments is initialized in the same manner in
ALL experiment. ALL experiment is forced by historical forcings for the period 1920–2005 and
by the CMIP5 RCP8.5 scenario for the period 2006–210053. Both XGHG and XAER experiments
use the same forcing protocol, except that either greenhouse gas or aerosol concentrations are held
fixed at the 1920’s condition. The temporal evolution of global-mean surface air temperature from
1920 to 2080 is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 8. ALL experiment shows a steady warming

before the year 1980 is much weaker than the one afterward, with a large variability. The warming
trend in ALL experiment (-0.62 K decade-1) is well captured by the linear sum of the GHG and
AER experiments (GHG+AER; -0.62 K decade-1), supporting the use of these experiments to
attribute forced responses. They are compared to an 1800-year pre-industrial control simulation
(piControl), which is used to estimate the internal climate variability.

intensity are quantified by computing the ensemble-mean differences between the two experiments,
i.e., ALL-XAER (referred to as AER experiment) and ALL-XGHG (referred to as GHG

isolates that of greenhouse gas forcing. Although 40 members are available for ALL experiment,
only the first 20 members are analyzed to make a fair comparison to XGHG and XAER experiment.

CESM2 single-forcing LENS simulations consist of 20 ensemble members of anthropogenic
aerosol-only (AAER) experiments, and 15 ensemble members of greenhouse gas-only (GHG)
experiments. To maintain consistency, the first 15 ensembles from both experiments are analyzed.
Each experiment spans from 1920 to 2050, which is shorter than the period covered by CESM1
LENS, based on historical (1920–2014) and SSP3-7.0 (2015–2050) scenarios.

In the study, the authors first quantify the change in the strength of the northern- and southern-hemisphere Hadley Circulation (HC) under historic and projected aerosol, greenhouse gas, and all-forcing scenarios in the CESM1 large ensemble. The authors find that the northern HC weakens under the all-forcing scenario from 1920-2080, while the change in the southern HC is indistinguishable from natural variability. I found the analysis contained within the study to be sound and that the topic potentially falls within the scope of Nature Communications. ### Reviewer 2

The authors explore the potential influence of anthropogenic aerosol (AA) forcing on the Northern Hemisphere (NH) hadley cell weakening from 1970 to 2080 based on single forcing simulations from various climate models. Their analyses reveal that about 40% of the NH Hadley cell weakening is attributed to the decline in AA. Based on the KE equation decomposition, they further demonstrate that the weakening is linked to diabatic heating patterns asymmetrically placed in the two hemispheres.
The analyses based on KE equation is interesting, but I have a fundamental concern about this manuscript, where the authors seem to oversimplify the aerosol emission to be simply “decline” since 1970, which is a bit outdated compared to relevant studies published in recent years. It is true that the global-mean aerosol concentration has been continuously decreasing since the 1970s. However, the declines only occur in Europe and North America, while emissions in other regions, especially East and South Asia, kept increasing, which seems to be less discussed in the introduction. Actually, many of the cited studies discussing global-mean aerosol forcings were published about ten years ago, so some of the discussions on hemispheric aerosol imbalance seem to be outdated.
Many studies have emphasized the complex co-impacts of regional aerosol forcings due to the strong spatial heterogeneity (e.g., [1-8]), in that different regional aerosol forcings could have distinct teleconnections to the large-scale circulations. For example, the Hadley cell discussed in this manuscript is sensitive to the latitudinal locations of forcings, and the aerosol forcings in Asia and Europe since the 1970s are located at distinct zonal and meridional locations, which should have very different dynamical impacts on the Northern Hemisphere Hadley cell ([3]).
Moreover, since the authors also include the future projections up to 2080, it is worth noting that the emissions between East Asia and South Asia started to show different trends since the recent decade as well, which further increases the complexity (e.g., Ref.[9-11]). So recently many efforts have been made to diagnose the impacts of more aerosol forcings (e.g., RAMIP; [8-9]), and the RCP emission scenario seems to be outdated to diagnose the future impacts of aerosols.
Therefore, I am concerned that the authors’ attribution to “decline of aerosol forcing” oversimplified the dynamical mechanisms behind the large-scale circulation responses. Although the energy analyses are interesting, I am concerned this study might not be novel and robust enough to extend the current understanding of anthropogenic aerosols, to be honest….

## Paper

## Abstract

The Hadley circulation plays a key role in transporting atmospheric heat from the tropics to the
subtropics, shaping the climate in low latitudes. While its projected weakening has been largely
attributed to rising greenhouse gas concentrations, the long-term impact of future anthropogenic
aerosol concentrations remains underexplored. Here, we show that the projected changes in
anthropogenic aerosol concentrations can account for about one-third of the Northern Hemisphere
Hadley circulation weakening between 1980 and 2080, emerging as a major driver of tropical
circulation change throughout the 21st century. This impact is linked to altered diabatic heating
patterns in the northern tropics, driven by precipitation changes under reduced aerosol forcing.
These results highlight a critical trade-off of aerosol mitigation: while improving air quality, it may
amplify tropical atmospheric circulation changes driven by greenhouse gases.

---

## Introduction

The Hadley Circulation (HC) consists of ascending motion in the deep tropics, poleward flow in
the upper troposphere, descending motion in the subtropics, and equatorward return flow near the
surface. This thermally direct overturning circulation strongly influences tropical hydroclimate
and maintains subtropical dry zones1–4. As global warming accelerates, climate model simulations
consistently project a weakening of the Northern Hemisphere (NH) HC from the past to the future
climate5–9. This weakening has primarily been attributed to changes in anthropogenic greenhouse
gases and aerosols6,10–17.

While the weakening of the HC by increasing greenhouse gases is well documented, the response
of the HC to changing aerosols is not well understood as it is sensitive to the analysis period and
models due to the complex spatiotemporal evolution of aerosol forcing10,15,18. Anthropogenic
aerosols increased globally until the 1980s, particularly after the end of World War II, but have
since followed divergent regional trajectories: declining in Europe and North America due to
effective mitigation efforts but continuing to increase in East and South Asia19–24 (Supplementary
Fig. 1). Past studies utilizing climate model simulations in different configurations have shown
that the overall cooling effect of increasing anthropogenic aerosols has likely strengthened the HC
in the NH, counteracting the weakening induced by greenhouse warming10,17,25. However, the
impacts of anthropogenic aerosols over the past few decades are uncertain, as aerosol
concentrations have declined in the Western Hemisphere but increased in the Eastern Hemisphere.
While these zonally asymmetric aerosol forcings may have competed with each other, recent
studies have suggested that changes in HC intensity are more sensitive to aerosol changes in the
Western Hemisphere, thereby driving a likely weakening of the HC since the 1980s16,21,23. Despite
these findings, the impact of time-varying aerosol forcings (Supplementary Fig. 1) on HC intensity
change is not well quantified. The relative importance of anthropogenic aerosols compared to
greenhouse gases and their underlying mechanism(s) also remains poorly understood.

In this work, we show the pivotal role of anthropogenic aerosol forcing in driving intensity changes
of the NH HC. By examining large ensembles of single-forcing climate model simulations, we
identify the mechanisms underlying aerosol-induced HC intensity changes and compare them with
those driven by greenhouse gases. As the impacts of aerosols on atmospheric circulation changes
are often obscure and model-dependent26–28, the robustness of the results is also tested by
employing a multi-model framework and an additional suite of the latest large-ensemble
simulations.

---

Each ensemble member in XGHG and XAER experiments is initialized in the same manner in

LENS, based on historical (1920–2014) and SSP3-7.0 (2015–2050) scenarios.

Although CESM2 LENS is the latest single-forcing large ensemble experiments, this study
primarily analyses CESM1-LENS. This is because it has a longer temporal coverage (extending
to 2080) and larger ensemble size (20 members), both of which are essential for robustly detecting
long-term forced responses and identifying the underlying physical mechanisms.

CMIP6 DAMIP

In addition to CESM1 LENS, we use model output from the Detection and Attribution Model
Intercomparison Project (DAMIP)37 of CMIP657. DAMIP provides single-forcing simulations that
isolate the effects of individual forcing agents, including anthropogenic aerosols and greenhouse
gases, in both historical and future climates. This dataset allows us to assess whether the HC
response to aerosol forcings is consistent across a broader set of models. Specifically, four models
which provide both the historical aerosol-only (hist-aer) and GHG-only (hist-GHG) simulations
for 1850–2020, as well as their respective future scenarios (ssp245-aer and ssp245-GHG) for
2021–2100, are used. They are CanESM5, GISS-E2-1-G, MIROC6, and NorESM2-LM. Historical
simulation for 1850–2014 and SSP2-4.5 scenario simulation for 2015–2100 are also examined to

ensemble member from each model (r1i1p1f2 for GISS-E2-1-G and r1i1p1f1 for the others) is

one ensemble member from each model is utilized to avoid overpresentation of models with larger
ensembles, the results do not change significantly when all available ensemble members are used.

It is important to note that the aerosol scenarios differ between the model experiments. DAMIP
follows the SSP2-4.5 aerosol pathway, while XAER experiment in CESM1 LENS and aerosol-
only experiment in CESM2 LENS are based on the RCP8.5 and SSP3-7.0 aerosol scenarios,
respectively. As such, comparisons between CESM1 LENS, CESM2 LENS, and DAMIP should
be interpreted qualitatively.

### Reviewer 1

I have completed my review of “Anthropogenic Aerosol Decline Substantially Amplifies Northern Hadley Circulation Weakening in the 21st century” by S.-Y. Kim et. al., submitted 2025 to Nature Communications.
In the study, the authors first quantify the change in the strength of the northern- and southern-hemisphere Hadley Circulation (HC) under historic and projected aerosol, greenhouse gas, and all-forcing scenarios in the CESM1 large ensemble. They attribute this decline in the northern hemisphere HC to a combination of GHG and anthropogenic forcings through use of the CESM1 single-forcing large ensemble simulations. The authors then utilize a Kuo-Eliassen decomposition to separate changes in the overturning streamfunction into contributions from diabatic heating, eddy heat flux, eddy momentum flux, zonal friction terms, and changes in static stability. I found the analysis contained within the study to be sound and that the topic potentially falls within the scope of Nature Communications. However this manuscript does not clearly articulate the key result(s) of the study, and how they are significant to the field. Therefore I recommend a major revision before this manuscript is accepted for publication. I have included additional comments below that I hope the authors will use to strengthen the manuscript.

In other words, I am not surprised to see a significant trend in the NH HC under the ALL-xAER scenario. Instead, I am much more interested in why this would be the case.
I believe that the authors’ use of the Kuo-Eliassen equation is useful perspective from which to address this question. ### Reviewer 2

The authors explore the potential influence of anthropogenic aerosol (AA) forcing on the Northern Hemisphere (NH) hadley cell weakening from 1970 to 2080 based on single forcing simulations from various climate models. Their analyses reveal that about 40% of the NH Hadley cell weakening is attributed to the decline in AA. Based on the KE equation decomposition, they further demonstrate that the weakening is linked to diabatic heating patterns asymmetrically placed in the two hemispheres.
The analyses based on KE equation is interesting, but I have a fundamental concern about this manuscript, where the authors seem to oversimplify the aerosol emission to be simply “decline” since 1970, which is a bit outdated compared to relevant studies published in recent years. It is true that the global-mean aerosol concentration has been continuously decreasing since the 1970s. However, the declines only occur in Europe and North America, while emissions in other regions, especially East and South Asia, kept increasing, which seems to be less discussed in the introduction. Actually, many of the cited studies discussing global-mean aerosol forcings were published about ten years ago, so some of the discussions on hemispheric aerosol imbalance seem to be outdated.
Many studies have emphasized the complex co-impacts of regional aerosol forcings due to the strong spatial heterogeneity (e.g., [1-8]), in that different regional aerosol forcings could have distinct teleconnections to the large-scale circulations. For example, the Hadley cell discussed in this manuscript is sensitive to the latitudinal locations of forcings, and the aerosol forcings in Asia and Europe since the 1970s are located at distinct zonal and meridional locations, which should have very different dynamical impacts on the Northern Hemisphere Hadley cell ([3]).
Moreover, since the authors also include the future projections up to 2080, it is worth noting that the emissions between East Asia and South Asia started to show different trends since the recent decade as well, which further increases the complexity (e.g., Ref.[9-11]). So recently many efforts have been made to diagnose the impacts of more aerosol forcings (e.g., RAMIP; [8-9]), and the RCP emission scenario seems to be outdated to diagnose the future impacts of aerosols.
Therefore, I am concerned that the authors’ attribution to “decline of aerosol forcing” oversimplified the dynamical mechanisms behind the large-scale circulation responses. Although the energy analyses are interesting, I am concerned this study might not be novel and robust enough to extend the current understanding of anthropogenic aerosols, to be honest….

Line 106: Some recent studies have conducted inter-model comparisons of aerosol forcings (e.g., [10]), which are worth referring to.

Line 291: I am not quite sure if I understand the authors’ argument correctly, but the claim of “one-to-one comparison between the experiments” are incorrect for me. Although the single forcing simulations are branched from the ALL experiment, they are different “worlds” when forcings are changed since the internal variability changes after the first few decades. Line 317: Same as the previous comment. Intuitively, all ensemble members should be used to calculate the ensemble mean, in my opinion.

## Paper

## Abstract

The Hadley circulation plays a key role in transporting atmospheric heat from the tropics to the
subtropics, shaping the climate in low latitudes. While its projected weakening has been largely
attributed to rising greenhouse gas concentrations, the long-term impact of future anthropogenic
aerosol concentrations remains underexplored. Here, we show that the projected changes in
anthropogenic aerosol concentrations can account for about one-third of the Northern Hemisphere
Hadley circulation weakening between 1980 and 2080, emerging as a major driver of tropical
circulation change throughout the 21st century. This impact is linked to altered diabatic heating
patterns in the northern tropics, driven by precipitation changes under reduced aerosol forcing.
These results highlight a critical trade-off of aerosol mitigation: while improving air quality, it may
amplify tropical atmospheric circulation changes driven by greenhouse gases.

---

## Introduction

The Hadley Circulation (HC) consists of ascending motion in the deep tropics, poleward flow in
the upper troposphere, descending motion in the subtropics, and equatorward return flow near the
surface. This thermally direct overturning circulation strongly influences tropical hydroclimate
and maintains subtropical dry zones1–4. As global warming accelerates, climate model simulations
consistently project a weakening of the Northern Hemisphere (NH) HC from the past to the future
climate5–9. This weakening has primarily been attributed to changes in anthropogenic greenhouse
gases and aerosols6,10–17.

While the weakening of the HC by increasing greenhouse gases is well documented, the response
of the HC to changing aerosols is not well understood as it is sensitive to the analysis period and
models due to the complex spatiotemporal evolution of aerosol forcing10,15,18. Anthropogenic
aerosols increased globally until the 1980s, particularly after the end of World War II, but have
since followed divergent regional trajectories: declining in Europe and North America due to
effective mitigation efforts but continuing to increase in East and South Asia19–24 (Supplementary
Fig. 1). Past studies utilizing climate model simulations in different configurations have shown
that the overall cooling effect of increasing anthropogenic aerosols has likely strengthened the HC
in the NH, counteracting the weakening induced by greenhouse warming10,17,25. However, the
impacts of anthropogenic aerosols over the past few decades are uncertain, as aerosol
concentrations have declined in the Western Hemisphere but increased in the Eastern Hemisphere.
While these zonally asymmetric aerosol forcings may have competed with each other, recent
studies have suggested that changes in HC intensity are more sensitive to aerosol changes in the
Western Hemisphere, thereby driving a likely weakening of the HC since the 1980s16,21,23. Despite
these findings, the impact of time-varying aerosol forcings (Supplementary Fig. 1) on HC intensity
change is not well quantified. The relative importance of anthropogenic aerosols compared to
greenhouse gases and their underlying mechanism(s) also remains poorly understood.

In this work, we show the pivotal role of anthropogenic aerosol forcing in driving intensity changes
of the NH HC. By examining large ensembles of single-forcing climate model simulations, we
identify the mechanisms underlying aerosol-induced HC intensity changes and compare them with
those driven by greenhouse gases. As the impacts of aerosols on atmospheric circulation changes
are often obscure and model-dependent26–28, the robustness of the results is also tested by
employing a multi-model framework and an additional suite of the latest large-ensemble
simulations.

---

## Results

Hadley circulation weakening due to anthropogenic forcings

The HC intensity changes, derived from the CESM1 large ensemble single-forcing experiment
(CESM1 LENS), are presented in Fig. 1. Under all-forcing scenario (ALL experiment; See
Methods), the NH HC intensity (Ψ ) shows robust weakening from 1920 to 2080 at a rate of -
max
0.62×109 kg s-1decade-1 (Table 1). This is consistent with a previous study6. The time of emergence
of NH HC intensity change, determined by the year when the forced response exceeds the range
of natural variability29–31, is estimated to be around 2020. The natural variability is defined as the
one-standard-deviation range of Ψ in the pre-industrial simulation (green lines in Fig. 1a).
max
The long-term change is less pronounced in the Southern Hemisphere (SH) HC intensity (Ψ ).
min
From 1920 through 2080, Ψ remains within the bounds of the internal variability (Fig. 1b). This
min
result reinforces the finding that the HC weakening is more pronounced in the NH than in the
SH6,12. This hemispheric asymmetry is consistent with prior studies and may be related to
differences in aerosol distributions and stratospheric ozone27,32.

The intensity of the NH HC (hereafter referred to as HC unless otherwise specified) exhibits a
distinct decadal variation (Fig. 1a). Specifically, the trend switches sign around 1980, transitioning
from a strengthening phase prior to the 1970s to a weakening phase thereafter (Table 1). The recent
weakening is consistent with observations5, although it is less clear in reanalyses33,34. As shown
below, this transition is likely associated with changes in aerosol emissions in the NH
(Supplementary Fig. 1; See also refs.16,23,35,36).

The contribution of increasing greenhouse gas concentrations to the HC intensity change is
quantified by taking a difference between ALL and fixed greenhouse gas concentrations (XGHG)
experiments, denoted as GHG experiment (red in Fig. 1c; See Methods). The HC intensity trend
in GHG experiment is statistically significant over the analysis period (1920–2080) but is smaller
than the trend in ALL experiment. Even during the period of 1980–2080 when greenhouse-gas-
induced HC weakening accelerates, the trend is only ~60% of that in ALL experiment (Table 1).
The time of emergence in GHG experiment is also delayed by about 20 years compared to that in
ALL experiment (compare crossing of green lines in Fig. 1c with Fig. 1a). This suggests that
increasing greenhouse gases do not fully explain the HC weakening in ALL experiment, indicating
a substantial influence of anthropogenic aerosols.

The contribution of anthropogenic aerosols is quantified by differencing ALL from fixed
anthropogenic aerosols (XAER) experiments, denoted as AER (blue in Fig. 1c; See Methods).
While the aerosol-induced HC intensity change lies within the natural variability for the entire
period (1920–2080), statistically significant trends are observed in two distinct sub-periods (Table
1): the earlier period (1920–1980) when anthropogenic aerosols increased globally
(Supplementary Fig. 1), and the subsequent period (1981–2080) of anthropogenic aerosols decline,
especially in the Western Hemisphere36. During 1920–1980, increasing aerosol concentrations
strengthened the HC intensity by 0.47×109 kg s-1decade-1, which exceeds the trend in the ALL
experiment. After 1980, declining aerosol concentrations weaken the HC by -0.35×109 kg s-1
decade-1, accounting for approximately 34% of the total HC weakening in the ALL experiment
over 1980–2080 (Table 1). Since the latter weakening effect after 1980 outweighs the former
strengthening effect before 1980, the net impact of anthropogenic aerosol forcing on HC intensity
over the entire analysis period is an overall weakening (Table 1). The results are robust to the
specific choice of transition year within the 1970–1980 period, as NH aerosol emissions were in a
transition phase during this decade (Supplementary Fig. 1).

It is important to note that aerosol effect is not always secondary. In certain periods, it acts as the
dominant driver of HC intensity changes. For instance, during the earlier phase of aerosol decline
(1980–2040), the aerosol-induced HC weakening (-0.56109 kg s-1 decade-1) is more pronounced
than the greenhouse-gas-induced weakening (-0.34109 kg s-1 decade-1). This underscores the
time-dependent nature of aerosol forcing and its critical role in shaping near-term tropical
circulation changes.

The combined effects of greenhouse gases and aerosols are further evaluated by comparing the
trend derived from the linear sum of the GHG and AER experiments (GHG + AER; purple in Fig.
1c) with that from the ALL experiment (black in Fig. 1a). The two time series are quantitatively
similar, showing close agreement across the three investigated periods (Table 1). This result
indicates that anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols are the two primary factors governing
the HC intensity changes from 1920 to 2080, consistent with ref.36.

The above results, derived from a single model, are supported by multi-model analyses. The multi-
model mean from the models participating in the CMIP6 Detection and Attribution Model
Intercomparison Project (DAMIP; See Methods)37 shows qualitatively similar results, despite
different experiment design and aerosol forcing (Table 1; See also Supplementary Fig. 3). In all-
forcing experiments, HC intensity exhibits a slight strengthening during 1920–1980, followed by
a weakening during 1980–2080. Approximately 26% of HC weakening is attributed to aerosol
reductions: -1.13×109 kg s-1 decade-1 in all forcing experiments versus -0.29×109 kg s-1 decade-1
in aerosol-only experiments over 1980–2080.

The robustness of HC intensity changes is also tested by examining the latest CESM2 large
ensemble single-forcing experiment (CESM2 LENS; See Methods). This experiment differs from
CESM1 LENS in that greenhouse gas or aerosol forcings are prescribed with all other forcings
held fixed at the 1850’s levels. Despite this difference, as well as differences in aerosol emission
scenarios, ensemble size, and integration length, qualitatively similar results are obtained
(Supplementary Fig. 4). The anthropogenic aerosol-only experiment in CESM2 LENS shows a
statistically significant HC strengthening of 0.43109 kg s-1 decade-1 for 1920–1980, and a
subsequent weakening of -0.48109 kg s-1 decade-1 for 1980–2050. This result is consistent with
the findings from both CESM1 LENS and CMIP6 DAMIP results (Table 1).

Physical processes of Hadley circulation weakening

While both increasing greenhouse gas concentrations and decreasing aerosol concentrations
contribute to the HC weakening during 1980–2080, their underlying mechanisms may differ. The
latitudinal-pressure structure of mass streamfunction (Ψ) indeed shows distinctively different

CESM1 LENS

A set of CESM1 55 large ensemble (LENS) simulations with a 1° spatial resolution 36 is analyzed
in this study. These simulations consist of 1) a 40-member ensemble simulation with all forcings
(ALL), 2) a 20-member ensemble simulation with time-fixed aerosol concentrations (XAER), and
3) a 20-member ensemble simulation with time-fixed greenhouse gas concentrations (XGHG).
Each ensemble member in XGHG and XAER experiments is initialized in the same manner in
ALL experiment. ALL experiment is forced by historical forcings for the period 1920–2005 and
by the CMIP5 RCP8.5 scenario for the period 2006–210053. Both XGHG and XAER experiments
use the same forcing protocol, except that either greenhouse gas or aerosol concentrations are held
fixed at the 1920’s condition. The temporal evolution of global-mean surface air temperature from
1920 to 2080 is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 8. ALL experiment shows a steady warming
trend from the past to the future, being the warming intensity sensitive to the period. The warming
before the year 1980 is much weaker than the one afterward, with a large variability. The warming
trend in ALL experiment (-0.62 K decade-1) is well captured by the linear sum of the GHG and
AER experiments (GHG+AER; -0.62 K decade-1), supporting the use of these experiments to
attribute forced responses. They are compared to an 1800-year pre-industrial control simulation
(piControl), which is used to estimate the internal climate variability.

The impacts of greenhouse gases and aerosols forcings on the past and future changes in the HC
intensity are quantified by computing the ensemble-mean differences between the two experiments,
i.e., ALL-XAER (referred to as AER experiment) and ALL-XGHG (referred to as GHG
experiment). AER experiment isolates the effect of aerosol forcing, while the GHG experiment
isolates that of greenhouse gas forcing. Although 40 members are available for ALL experiment,
only the first 20 members are analyzed to make a fair comparison to XGHG and XAER experiment.
The results from all 40 ensemble members in ALL experiment are quantitatively the same as those
from the first 20 members (Compare Fig. 1a to Supplementary Fig. 9)

CESM2 LENS

A set of CESM2 LENS simulations56 is also examined. They differ from CESM1 LENS
simulations not only in model but also in experiment design. While CESM1 LENS uses an all-
but-one framework (i.e., XGHG and XAER), CESM2 LENS uses a forcing-only framework.
CESM2 single-forcing LENS simulations consist of 20 ensemble members of anthropogenic
aerosol-only (AAER) experiments, and 15 ensemble members of greenhouse gas-only (GHG)
experiments. To maintain consistency, the first 15 ensembles from both experiments are analyzed.
Each experiment spans from 1920 to 2050, which is shorter than the period covered by CESM1
LENS, based on historical (1920–2014) and SSP3-7.0 (2015–2050) scenarios.

Although CESM2 LENS is the latest single-forcing large ensemble experiments, this study
primarily analyses CESM1-LENS. This is because it has a longer temporal coverage (extending
to 2080) and larger ensemble size (20 members), both of which are essential for robustly detecting
long-term forced responses and identifying the underlying physical mechanisms.

CMIP6 DAMIP

In addition to CESM1 LENS, we use model output from the Detection and Attribution Model
Intercomparison Project (DAMIP)37 of CMIP657. DAMIP provides single-forcing simulations that
isolate the effects of individual forcing agents, including anthropogenic aerosols and greenhouse
gases, in both historical and future climates. This dataset allows us to assess whether the HC
response to aerosol forcings is consistent across a broader set of models. Specifically, four models
which provide both the historical aerosol-only (hist-aer) and GHG-only (hist-GHG) simulations
for 1850–2020, as well as their respective future scenarios (ssp245-aer and ssp245-GHG) for
2021–2100, are used. They are CanESM5, GISS-E2-1-G, MIROC6, and NorESM2-LM. Historical
simulation for 1850–2014 and SSP2-4.5 scenario simulation for 2015–2100 are also examined to
provide a more comprehensive comparison with CESM1 LENS. For consistency, only the first
ensemble member from each model (r1i1p1f2 for GISS-E2-1-G and r1i1p1f1 for the others) is
used for the common period 1920–2080 for a direct comparison among the simulations. Although
one ensemble member from each model is utilized to avoid overpresentation of models with larger
ensembles, the results do not change significantly when all available ensemble members are used.

It is important to note that the aerosol scenarios differ between the model experiments. DAMIP
follows the SSP2-4.5 aerosol pathway, while XAER experiment in CESM1 LENS and aerosol-
only experiment in CESM2 LENS are based on the RCP8.5 and SSP3-7.0 aerosol scenarios,
respectively. As such, comparisons between CESM1 LENS, CESM2 LENS, and DAMIP should
be interpreted qualitatively.

Many studies have emphasized the complex co-impacts of regional aerosol forcings due to the strong spatial heterogeneity (e.g., [1-8]), in that different regional aerosol forcings could have distinct teleconnections to the large-scale circulations. For example, the Hadley cell discussed in this manuscript is sensitive to the latitudinal locations of forcings, and the aerosol forcings in Asia and Europe since the 1970s are located at distinct zonal and meridional locations, which should have very different dynamical impacts on the Northern Hemisphere Hadley cell ([3]).
Moreover, since the authors also include the future projections up to 2080, it is worth noting that the emissions between East Asia and South Asia started to show different trends since the recent decade as well, which further increases the complexity (e.g., Ref.[9-11]).
